July 2009 ## Green Shoots or a False Dawn? - After a very poor Q1 things have only marginally improved in Q2. Our initial estimate is that copper wirerod consumption fell by 11.8% in H1 compared to H1 2008, with wire and cable production 11.7% lower, with the rate of decline just under 10% in Q2. The winding wire sector continues to be worst hit with consumption down by 17.9%. - The developed world continues to be gripped by recession and the most optimistic view here is that the bottom has been reached and that markets have stabilised. However, in the developing world there are definitely some signs of a recovery. The Chinese market has picked up, with domestic demand growth compensating for continued very weak exports of both wire and cable and electrical appliances and equipment. There are also signs of a recovery starting in India. - These positive signs are very welcome to the beleaguered cable industry, but it is definitely too early to call a sustainable recovery based on these patchy “green shoots”. What is a worry is that when the badly hit winding, automotive and appliance wire sectors begin to recover, the lack of new commercial construction projects, continuing poor residential construction and a general reduction in investment, will offset this recovery and prolong the cable industry’s woes into 2010. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 12 July 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Europe Our initial estimates show that in Q2 copper wirerod production amounted to 716,000t and that of wire and cable to 613,000t. For the first 6 months of 2009 wirerod production contracted by 24.5% and wire and cable production by 23.0% y-o-y. Currently, there is a mixed picture across the European wire & cable industry, with lower copper prices in Q1 not enough to counterbalance the significant slowdown in construction activity. Apart from the economic slowdown, Europe also experienced a cold winter which impacted the construction and communication wire segments. Medium voltage cable demand has begun to be affected by investment uncertainty amongst electricity companies in the private sector, but demand for high voltage and submarine cables remains good as they are less influenced, at least in the short term. Challenged by the tough market conditions, fabricators are operating under a lower cost base and looking to concentrate on high-value added businesses, less exposed to economic cyclical trends. The **International Wrought Copper Council** anticipates that cable order intake in the automotive and winding wire sectors will fall by 50% in 2009. The hardest hit will be Western Europe but Eastern Europe will also suffer as some harnesses producers migrate to North Africa. CRU anticipates that a slow recovery will take place in Eastern Europe, Germany and Italy, and an even slower one in the UK, Spain and Russia. ### **Current issues from the wirerod market** **Aurubis** said that Q1 was disappointing and the seasonal demand rise in spring was not realised. The company said that a 50% y-o-y contraction in w

ire & cable order intake occurred in Q1. Stable demand from the utility power sector prevented further deterioration in wirerod sales. However, Aurubis believes that it has seen the bottom, with February having been the gloomiest month. The company then saw signs of improvement in May and June, and, as a result, postponed its short-term working plans at its wirerod plant in Hamburg. ### **…and the cable market** **Draka** experienced a 23% y-o-y fall in sales volume in the first four months of 2009, with some stabilisation signs evident since April. Cost measures have been announced, targeted mainly to the communications unit, but energy & infrastructure is also affected. Along with earlier announcements, job cuts amount to 1,500 or 15% of the workforce. The sales volume in H1 2009 is expected to fall substantially and this will impact capacity utilisation and profitability. Due to the slump in European construction activity, shipments to Spain, Finland and Estonia were hit, but better performance was achieved in Benelux. The energy & infrastructure and industry & specialty units sales are anticipated to fall by 20-30% in H1 2009 whilst those of data communication cables by 12-20%. **NKT** reported a 25% y-o-y decline in low voltage sales to the building and construction sector in Q1. Medium voltage offtake was also under pressure. But high voltage shipments performed well, with those of catenary wires up by 48% y-o-y. The new high voltage plant in Cologne is just coming on stream. **Prysmian** said that organic sales of energy cables fell by 10% y-o-y in Q1 and those of telecom cables by 20%. The high voltage market showed stable demand in Q1. The company expects weak demand in the trade & installer and power distribution businesses for the rest of the year. More resilient demand is expected from power transmission and industrial applications. **Essex** forecasts that European consumption in the winding wire market will slow by 30-40% in 2009. # North America 

### **Slow but steady in Q2** 

The US economy is showing signs of stabilising, and this has been reflected in wire and cable production and consumption.  Demand has been slow but steady so far this year.  In Q2, most segments were broadly flat against the first quarter, and all saw less marked year-on-year declines than in Q1.  Power utility cable and communications cable both saw production stay steady in Q2, although there was a further modest decline in winding wire.  Some wire and cable producers are now starting to feel optimistic that the market may have bottomed out, at least for certain applications, with manufacturing and automotive sectors no longer falling, and with the prospect of significantly more stimulus infrastructure spending still to come (only 9% has been spent so far, according to estimates from Deloitte).  However, there are significant concerns that the prospects for demand from the commercial construction sector could worsen. In the short run, activity will be hit due to numerous shutdowns over the 4<sup>th</sup> July (US) and 1<sup>st</sup> July (Canada) holidays, with some extended vacation shutdowns at customers. 

### **Manufacturing and automotive sectors show signs of improvement….** 

The Conference Board’s Index of Leading Indicators saw a second month of growth in May, increasing 1.2% m-o-m, following a 1.1% m-o-m increase in April.  This follows a sustained period of decline since July 2008.  Industrial production, however, was still down 1% y-o-y in May.  Capacity utilisation also fell to 65% in May (as opposed to 65.6% in April, and a long term average of nearly 80%).  However, there are signs that the manufacturing sector may slowly be turning a corner. Although shipments of manufactured durable goods were also still down 2.1% m-o-m in May, new orders were up 1.1% m-o-m, up for the third time in the last four months.  Inventories were also down 0.8% m-o-m in May, the fifth consecutive month of decline, a necessary step for eventual demand recovery.  In the automotive sector, production volumes continue to be well down on 2008 in Q2, with car production down 44% and commercial vehicle production down 52%.  However, they were up against the first quarter, suggesting they may have hit bottom.  Plans to introduce a scrapping incentive scheme of $3500-$4500 for old cars are also likely to lead to an improvement in sales, and ultimately production.  A similar scheme in Europe has given a significant boost to sales.  Despite these modest signs of improvement, nobody expects a speedy recovery. 

### **…but biggest risk to outlook is from construction sector** 

Wire and cable makers remain pessimistic, however, about the outlook from the construction sector, believing that there is a real threat that volumes could fall as commercial construction declines. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 7 of 12 July 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # North East Asia ### **Japan continues to struggle** The Japanese wirerod and wire and cable sectors continue to struggle in the face of very weak markets, with copper wirerod production in H1 down by an estimated 29% year-on-year, and copper wire and cable production falling by 28%. The worst performance is coming from the winding, appliance, and automotive wire sectors, where demand is down by between 40% and 50% as a result of a collapse in exports of electrical goods and equipment and the well publicised woes of the automotive industry. The latest data from the JCMA shows that copper cable shipments in May were down by 31.4% compared to May in 2008 and the total of 44,700 tonnes conductor was the lowest monthly total since February 1975. The construction sector was particularly weak with shipments here at their lowest level for 26 years. ### **H1 turns out better than expected in South Korea** Our initial estimates for H1 of this year in South Korea show that both copper wirerod and wire and cable production was much stronger than the other countries in this region, and ahead of our forecasts at the start of the year. Wirerod production has been particularly strong with Q1 on a par with Q1 2008, and Q2 seeing a rise in output compared to a significant fall in Q2 last year. This has been driven by both healthy demand from local cablemakers, and also strong export demand from China. Copper wire and cable production was flat year-on-year in H1, which is the best performance amongst any developed world country. The main driver of this growth has been the power cable sector. In Korea there is little use of aluminium even for utility power cables, and the local utility Kepco has been encouraged by the government to increase its power cable purchases. However, it has not increased its overall investment budget but has instead brought forward orders. As a result it is spending over two thirds of its budget in the first half of the year. Consequentially we expect power cable demand to tail off significantly in the second half of the year, which will hit cable production. Power cable demand is also being helped by the US$11bn stimulus package. As the world’s major shipbuilding nation Korea has the world’s largest market for ships cables, and despite the fact that orders for new ships have all but dried up, the main yards all have full order books out to at least 2011. This means that demand for ships cable will stay str

ong at least through 2010 and 2011, although it is then likely to fall sharply. On the downside the construction sector remains weak and this is impacting on building wire and LAN cable demand. Also the automotive sector has been hit hard by falling vehicle output. South Korea is one of the leading nations in terms of installing fibre in the local loop, and as a result the market for external copper telecom is disappearing fast. ### **Taiwan remains depressed** In Taiwan all the main wire and cable product sectors have seen sharply lower demand in the first half of 2009. Winding and electronic wire production has fallen by between 40% and 50%, with falling demand for exported electrical and electronic equipment being the main reason for this. Overall we estimate that copper wire and cable production was 26% lower year-on-year in H1, although some possible comfort can be drawn from the fact that there was an improvement in Q2 compared to Q1. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 8 of 12 July 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** |North East A|sian co

© 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 9 of 12 July 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Rest of World ### **Chinese outlook continues to improve** China is continuing to import large volumes of refined copper, with implied refined copper consumption up by over 40% year-on-year in the first five months of 2009. However, we still believe that a large part of this growth is not truly reflected in actual copper rod that is being consumed to produce wire and cable for customers. Based on our analysis of the market we estimate that true copper rod consumption, excluding stocking and other effects, was up by 4.0% in H1, with copper wire and cable production rising by 3.3% to 1,921,000 tonnes. The Chinese economy does seem to be gathering pace, and there is now a strong chance that a sustained recovery is already underway, but there are still opposing forces at work. Whilst export demand remains very weak for both wire and cable and cable containing products, government policies to stimulate domestic consumption appear to be working. Fixed asset investment growth accelerated further in May and is now growing at its fastest rate since early 2004. In the construction sector commercial property sales increased by 75.5% in May and construction activity seems to be recovering quite strongly with both completions and areas under construction starting to pick up since March. Vehicle production has grown by 12.2% in the first five months of 2009 compared to the same period in 2008, with the government funded trade-in subsidies being extended and increased from RMB1bn to RMB5bn. RMB2bn has also been allocated to a new home appliance trade-in subsidy which should help support production of domestic appliances, but so far in the first five months of 2009 production of washing machines, refrigerators and freezers has risen by a modest 3.7% year-onyear. Power cable demand is continuing to be supported by infrastructure spending, although the strongest demand is still for the higher voltage cables. Production of power generation equipment grew by 8.0% year-on-year t

o May in terms of total Mwh, but electricity generation continues to run below last years numbers. In May 2009 it was 2.7% lower than in May 2008 and for the first five months was 4.0% lower. There are signs though that industrial production growth is starting to gather pace, and we have revised up our forecast for this year to growth of 8.2%. 

### **Indian outlook also improving** 

As with China, the Indian economy seems to be starting to recover from the effects of the economic crisis, and as a result the outlook for the wire and cable sector continues to improve. One of the advantages for the Indian cable industry is that demand is very much driven by the domestic market, and is much less reliant on the export sector than China. The expansion of the country’s power infrastructure will continue and although the real estate sector has slowed due to the economic crisis, this will be a much shallower and shorter slump than in the developed world, with a recovery expected in the second half of this year. Indian industrial production is also forecast to continue to grow with a modest rise of 0.3% this year followed by growth of 6.4% in 2010. For Indian wirerod producers demand has also been sustained by the continuing replacement of poor quality scrap based rod, with better quality product, both due to the gaining of market share by better quality cable manufacturers which use better quality rod, and also reduced output from low quality producers due to problems in scrap supplies and financing.

The plant is due to begin operation by the end of this year and will be the third new large rod mill established in the region in the last couple of years. **SWCC Showa Holdings Co** . announced it is to increase its Chinese magnet wire production to seven times the 2008 level by 2010. It plans to raise its stake in local JV Tianjin Showa Enamelled Wire Co. from the current 30% to 57%, turning it into a subsidiary. Production will be moved to a new 14,400 sq.m. plant in Tianjin which is scheduled to start operations in October, and the workforce will be doubled to 200. SWCC Showa is targeting an annual production of 12,000 tons of magnet wire in 2012 a

t the new facility. 

**El Sewedy Cables** is to establish a new LV energy cables plant in the Yemen, along with a local partner, in which it will have a 70% share. The plant will have an initial capacity of 12,000 tonnes a year. 

Italian cable manufacturer **Tratos Cavi** has bought UK LV energy cable manufacturer **North West Cables** , along with its subsidiary **Modular Wiring Systems Ltd** .
